segments.text: Commencing this week, we shall take a study in Paul's second letter to the Thessalonian
Christians.
During the last few weeks, we were considering Paul's first letter to the Thessalonian Christians.
And Church history tells us that the first letter to the Thessalonians was probably the
very first portion of the New Testament scriptures ever to be written.
It's very significant when we think of that, that the very first portion of the New Testament
scriptures relates to the second coming of Christ.
The second letter of Paul to the Thessalonians was written sometime subsequently, some years
later when Paul got news that though the Thessalonians had received his first letter, they were disturbed
by certain aspects of some teaching that they had received, some false teaching they had
received from other sources claiming to be apostolic, which had disturbed their spirit
in relation to the coming of Christ.
And this is the occasion for Paul's second letter.
And it's interesting to see how God has arranged these different circumstances to arise in
these different churches in the early days so that the apostle Paul could write to certain
specific circumstances that were found in local churches, but as a result of which,
unknown to himself perhaps, he was writing inspired scripture that was going to bless
millions of people in 20 centuries.
We think of Paul's letter to the Corinthians in a similar way where he wrote to them about
various matters concerning the gifts of the spirit because there was an abuse of the gifts
in the Corinthian church about marriage and various topics like that about the Lord's
table as a result of which we have certain clear guidelines today given us by the apostles.
So in a sense, we can say that even the disturbances and difficulties that cropped
up in these areas, legalism for example in Galatia, all these difficulties that the
devil brought were used by the Lord with a good purpose in the sense that the apostles
could lay down instruction which they would not have laid down if everything in every
church was going on perfectly.
And then we would have missed the benefit of that teaching.
So in a sense, if we understand it rightly, we can even give thanks to God that there
were these difficulties in those early churches so that as a result of which we could get
some clear teaching from the apostles on these matters.
And so in relation to the second coming of Christ, we have further teaching in second
Thessalonians concerning certain other aspects.
First of all, beginning at chapter one, verse one, again, Paul, Silas, and Timothy.
Sir Vanus is another word for Silas, to the church of the Thessalonians and God our Father
and the Lord Jesus Christ.
Paul is writing the letter, but as we considered in the first letter, he is humble enough
to associate Silas and Timothy, his co-workers, with him in the address because Paul recognized
he was only one member in the body of Christ.
This is something very interesting and important for us to see that in the New Testament, there
is no one man ministry.
Even when Paul writes a letter, he includes Silas and Timothy and says this letters from
all of us, even though every word of it is false.
He was one part of the body of Christ, so that team which comprise Silas and Timothy
and he did not despise them.
Unlike many who claim to be servants of God today, who seek to find an exalted position
for themselves in the eyes of others, he addresses it to the church of the Thessalonians and
God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, distinguishing clearly there between the Father
and the Son, which distinction the devil has tried to blur in these days by some who
teach that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are all the Lord Jesus Christ.
This is a heresy which is so subtle that we need to beware of God our Father and
the Lord Jesus Christ, two separate persons, one God in three persons.
Verse 2, grace to you and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
Notice this distinction between the persons of the Trinity that is constantly emphasized
in the New Testament episodes to counter this last day heresy that we find in these days
of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit being just the Lord Jesus Christ, which is a false teaching.
Verse 3, we ought always to give thanks to God for you.
It's amazing how Paul began his letters with a note of encouragement.
He was a true Father.
He wasn't always scolding and rebuking the children.
He was encouraging them saying, I thank God for you.
There are so many things in you which I really appreciate, even though they were false.
And that's an example for all earthly fathers to follow that when we exhort and have to
rebuke our children, let's ask ourselves whether we have also taken time to encourage
them by words of appreciation that we have given them when they deserve that.
So many fathers are quick to scold and rebuke and never do they give a word of encouragement.
But Paul was wise.
We are always to give thanks to God.
That was not just a psychological technique he was following.
It was the genuine expression of his heart.
He was sincerely thankful to God for the Christians in Thessalonica, as every one of us should
be thankful to God for our fellow believers.
It's because of our conceit and the pride in our flesh that we don't thank God for
one another more.
There's only one reason, dear friends, why we don't thank God for others more.
And that is our own pride and conceit.
If we were humble, we would be thankful to God that God has given us, brothers and
sisters, with all their weaknesses.
And they accept us with all our weaknesses.
We accept them with all their weaknesses.
We are thankful to God for them.
And he says here in verse 3, this is only fitting because your faith is greatly enlarged
and the love of each one of you all toward one another grows ever greater.
Paul was always delighted whenever he saw growth of faith and love.
You can look right through the Epistles of Paul and he was always emphasizing faith and
love.
Faith in God our Father, security in that love of God for us, faith, strong faith in
the Lord Jesus that's unshakable, and a fervent love for one another that nothing can
quench.
These are the two things which are more important than anything else in our life.
Faith in God, an fervent love for one another that should never be static but should always
be growing more and more and more and more and more and more.
And therefore he says in verse 4, therefore we ourselves speak proudly of you among the
churches of God.
You see, it's a Father who is taking delight in certain children who are manifesting such

Just like God himself was proud of such children who were reflecting the nature of Christ,
Paul himself was proud of them.
Now as you go on later in this letter you find that they had some confusion concerning
certain doctrines.
But that's not serious.
Paul can set that right.
He says that I can sort out.
But if it's a problem of faith and love, that's a serious problem which teaches us
that doctrinal error, though it is serious, it's not as serious as moral error.
True perfection is perfection in doctrine as well as in morals, but it's in our
model character that perfection must be pursued.
The other doctrinal error may sometimes merely be an intellectual problem where we can't understand
something right, but a model problem can make us lose our salvation.
And so we see here, he says, not only for your faith and love which grows tremendously
towards each other, but we're also praising God for your patience, your steadfastness,
your perseverance, that one word means all that.
Have faith in the midst of all your persecutions and afflictions which you endure.
It's one thing to have faith in the Lord and to praise God and to give thanks for
all things and to rejoice always when we are living a comfortable life, when everything
is going according to our wishes, we have no problems, no difficulties, no trials.
It's quite another thing to grow in faith and to endure in patience when we are afflicted
and when we have persecutions.
The Bible says in Acts 14, 22 that through much tribulation we must enter the kingdom
of God.
It is through tribulation that we enter God's kingdom.
There is no other way.
And so we are to look forward to tribulation as something which is our appointed lot on

mark of God's displeasure.
Far from it, it is a mark of God's pleasure over our life.

And so the Thessalonians suffered persecution because they were living a godly life, but
in spite of that their faith didn't waver.
On the contrary, verse 3 says their faith was greatly enlarged.
This is a result of the grace of God.
And also their love for one another did not grow cold in the days of persecution,
it became more fervent.
The more the devil hated them and troubled them, the more they loved one another and
the more their faith grew.
And he says in verse 5 that this manifestation of your faith and patience is a plain indication
of God's righteous judgment on the others so that you may be considered worthy of the
kingdom of God for which you are suffering.
We suffer for the sake of the kingdom of God.
There is a purpose in all our suffering and we manifest that we are worthy of that kingdom

We turn today to second Thessalonians chapter 1 and verse 4.
There in the last part of verse 4 we were considering last week about the faith and
patience of the Thessalonians Christians in the midst of all their persecutions and afflictions.
Or as another, the amplified translation puts it, their firm faith and endurance in the
midst of all the crushing distresses and persecutions under which you are holding up.
You see, faith and patience are two things that are joined together by God.
We told in Hebrews 6-12 that we inherit the promises not just through faith but through
faith and patience.
Many people have faith but they don't have patience and thereby prove that their faith
is really a dead faith.
If our faith were a living faith, it would always be manifested in patience.
That means we never give up because we believe that God is true to his word.
If I pray for something according to the will of God and I don't get the answer in
one or two days or one or two weeks and I give up, that clearly proves that I have
no faith at all.
I have a desire for the answer to prayer but I have no faith because I could not endure

The same thing applies in many aspects of faith.
The proof of our faith is in obedience to the word, as James says, faith without works

That's why God allows us to face trial and testing and persecution so that we can check

And so we see here, Paul says, I thank God for you, speak proudly of you because of
your faith and patience in the midst of all your crushing distresses.
Could Paul say that about you and me?
That he could boast about us to the other churches because he sees how we endure in
the midst of crushing distresses.
Sometimes a small little difficulty is enough to make us complain how we should be ashamed

faith. And he says further, as we considered last week, that this is a plain indication,
verse five, of God's righteous judgment because he is using all these testings to prepare you
for his kingdom. His aim is to show, to let you show yourselves worthy of his kingdom.
Or as Jamie Phillips says, without doubt, God intends to use your suffering to make
you worthy of his kingdom. Isn't that righteous of God? That that persecution which other people
are putting upon you, God can stop it very easily if he wants to, but he doesn't do it.
He allows other people to afflict you and to persecute you and thereby uses that evil of
the devil to work for your good by making it develop your character. That's why Paul says in
Romans five, we glory in tribulation, knowing that tribulation produces perseverance, and
that finally produces character. And that character is what God is after, and apparently
there's no other way to produce it except through persecution and affliction. And so we see
that God uses that to produce character in us. Once our eyes are open to this truth,
we shall no longer complain against these people who afflict us. But on the contrary,
we shall give thanks for them. We shall praise God that God has allowed them to treat us like this,

for after all, it's only just for God to repay with affliction those who afflict you.
Now it's very beautifully translated in the New English Bible where it says it's surely just

You see, God is the one who is going to balance the account in the final day.
So we don't have to balance the account. An eye for an eye was an Old Testament exhortation

Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do. We're not looking forward that they'll

he will also be righteous towards you by giving you relief who are being crushed with so many
